name: Fishbowl
use_case: A contested issue has to be talked through in front of a large audience, at a staff assembly, a parents' forum or a public meeting. A podium panel turns into a row of prepared statements and an open floor turns into chaos where the loudest win, so we want a handful of people to argue it out properly in full view, with the audience following closely and anyone who has something to add able to step into the conversation themselves.
strengths: a few voices can go deep on a contested question while hundreds follow every turn of the argument
an open seat lets anyone from the audience step in, so the line between speakers and listeners stays permeable
people in the circle speak to each other rather than to the audience, which discourages speeches
makes the reasoning behind positions visible to everyone, not just the conclusions
needs only chairs, a host and, in a large hall, a few microphones
weaknesses: most people in the room listen most of the time; it does not collect input from everyone
shy or junior participants rarely take the open seat in front of a crowd
confident regulars can occupy the inner circle unless the host enforces short turns
produces understanding and visible disagreement, not a decision
falls flat if the inner circle is staged with people who already agree
use_cases: The council has to hold a public meeting on a disputed plan to close a local school; officials answering questions from the floor last time ended in shouting, and this time residents and officials should actually debate it while the rest of the hall can join in.

A secondary-school teacher wants the class to practise arguing about a controversial text: a few students discuss it while the others watch closely, note how the argument develops, and then trade places.

Our conference panels are four experts reading out their slides one after another; the organisers want a live conversation on stage that audience members can step into rather than queue at a microphone.

At the staff assembly about the restructuring, management and employee representatives should discuss the hard questions openly in front of all two hundred colleagues instead of leadership presenting and taking a few questions.

Before the whole department adopts a new way of working, the colleagues who piloted it should talk frankly among themselves about what went well and what did not while everyone else listens and then asks questions.
audience: town hall and public meeting hosts
